title: Oral presentation structure
examples: How long should my introduction be for a presentation?
What is the best way to transition between my main points?
Can I use signposting words like 'firstly' and 'finally'?

explain.say: Today we will learn how to structure a good talk. A good talk has three main parts. These parts help your audience follow you easily.
The introduction grabs attention and tells the audience what you will talk about. You should start with a hook or a question.
The body of your talk covers your main points one by one. Each point needs clear support and examples to explain it.
The conclusion reminds the audience of your main message. You should summarize your key points briefly here.
Signposting words guide your listeners through your talk smoothly. Words like 'Firstly' and 'Next' help the audience follow your thoughts.
In real life, you use this structure when presenting a school project. You introduce your topic, give three main points with evidence, and then conclude strongly.

faq.q: How many main points should I include in my talk?
faq.a: Most presentations do well with three main points. This keeps the structure clear for the audience. You could also ask, 'Is three the magic number for points?' or 'How many topics should I cover?'
asks: Should I stick to three main ideas?

faq.q: What is the difference between a hook and an introduction?
faq.a: The hook is just the very beginning to grab attention. The introduction is the whole opening section that sets the stage. You could also ask, 'What should I say first?' or 'Is the hook the same as the intro?'

faq.q: Should I use signposting words all the time?
faq.a: No, use them when you move to a new section. They are helpful signposts, not constant chatter. You could also ask, 'When do I use linking words?' or 'Are signposts necessary?'
asks: How often should I use transition words?

faq.q: Is it better to write out my whole talk or use notes?
faq.a: It is best to use detailed notes rather than reading word for word. Notes help you sound natural and conversational. You could also ask, 'Should I memorize everything?' or 'What is the best way to prepare?'
asks: How much should I write down?

faq.q: If I run out of time, what should I do?
faq.a: If you are running short on time, focus only on your most important point. If you have extra time, you can expand on a good example. You could also ask, 'What if I finish too early?' or 'How do I manage my time?'
asks: What if I talk too long?
How do I pace my speech?

facts: A strong introduction clearly states the topic's scope.
The body of the talk must support the main idea with evidence.
Signposting words help the audience follow the speaker's logic.
A conclusion should leave the audience with a final, memorable thought.

quiz.say: What is the primary function of the introduction in a speech?
quiz.show: To grab attention and state the topic.

options.show: To grab attention and state the topic.
options.say: To grab attention and state the topic.

options.show: To list all the evidence points.
options.say: To list all the evidence points.

quiz.why: This sets expectations and hooks the audience immediately.

wrong.1: The conclusion is the final part, not explained first.
wrong.3: This belongs in the body, not the opening.

quiz.say: If you use the phrase 'In conclusion,' where in your speech should you place it?
quiz.show: At the very end of the talk.

options.show: In the middle of a point.
options.say: In the middle of a point.

options.show: At the very end of the talk.
options.say: At the very end of the talk.

quiz.why: This signals to the audience that the speech is wrapping up.

wrong.0: This confuses the audience about the main content.
wrong.1: It breaks the flow before the content even starts.
wrong.2: It sounds like you are ending too soon.

quiz.say: Which word is best used to move from the first point to the second?
quiz.why: This word clearly signals a sequence change to the listener.

wrong.0: Therefore shows a result, not just the next point.
wrong.1: This introduces evidence, not a new main point.
wrong.3: Finally means it is the last point, not the second.
